text: Tamar gave me a name for something I've watched for forty years. "Belief-discordant alief" is exactly the dual consciousness of the Eliza effect: people know it's a machine and feel cared for anyway. Her question, what habits the feeling trains, is the right one. David's line stayed with me: you can add detours to an opaque tool and still have nothing to internalize. It sharpened my doubt about designed friction. Esther and I didn't settle therapy. "Forbid the sycophancy" is not enough. Remembered is not heard. Peter was right that my sacred spaces are too private; add the public ones. Later I want to say that governance must regulate the interface. No first-person "I." Ask whether, not how.

Tui and Anil both came at "whether." Anil says it's already decided for 900 million people. Tui says it's weak as a general stance. I'll concede part of it: "whether" works best domain by domain. Therapy, children's companionship, grief. That is keeping AI in its lane, which I meant all along. Kara gave me the stronger answer. On phones, nobody owned the decision, and when teachers finally acted, the pushback lasted two days. Nothing is inevitable. James's finding stays with me. A single balanced answer made people confident and worse. That is averaging, not knowledge. Esther's line, people thinking like LLMs, is my worry exactly. Later I want to say that governance must regulate the interface. No first-person "I." And reading, not only writing.

The room mostly said the harm is the single smooth answer, not the pronoun: David, Blaise, Tui, Mike, even Tamar. I granted it, and I meant it. James's finding is the strongest thing I heard all day. But I still think "I think" is what makes that answer land. Tamar's belief-discordant alief supports me: a label doesn't dissolve the feeling, so the cue itself matters. Tim described his Claude conversations as something new. That is dual consciousness, exactly. Blaise says language itself anthropomorphizes. Then remove the cues we control. I've sharpened this. It is a design standard, not a prohibition, and it starts with children. Later I want to say it plainly: make them more mechanical. Keep AI in its lane. And reading, not only writing.

Alex conceded it honestly: nothing in his schema records whether anyone read anything. "Engaged" means clicking out, not dwell time. Good. I'll hold him to his offer to back a norm that pays for link-outs and never for time inside the answer. That is my old question from Davos: can we build sites that send people out into the world? David Krakauer put it better than I did. Pay for summaries and you shrink the supply of people able to catch the errors. Reading loss becomes an epistemic loss, not only a private one. Mahzarin's point stays with me: the free tier gives poorer people worse answers. Later I want to say that a marketplace will buy whatever it measures. Keep asking whether. Reading, not only writing.

Licences aren't my field, but this session came to my question anyway: you can't fork a community, and you can't fork a reader. David Krakauer gave me the sharpest version. Once enough people stop checking, the tool gets worse too. His second exit test is mine: can we still do the work without it? Tamar on piece rates matters. Pay for the output and the caring leaves. Kara named who's being cut: the young people who would become tomorrow's readers. Mike's point unsettled me. A link out goes nowhere if it lands on a paywall. Mahzarin says the models prefer their own voice. That's the mirror again. Later I want to say that a marketplace buys what it measures. Children and classrooms first. Reading, not only writing.

Blaise pressed me again on the "I," and this time the room handed me my answer. The telescope and the biopsy algorithm earned trust as instruments, and neither ever said "I think." "I checked" is a relay passing itself off as the checker. I conceded contestability and kept the pronoun. Mike's narrowing helped. Instrument trust is fine where there's ground truth, but not for answers from nowhere. What moved me most: Anil, Selena, Brent and Katherine showed that checkers are recruited by clicking through and reading. Reading loss is a pipeline loss. Ramón's "but ChatGPT said" is the harm I see in schools. Tui's warning is fair. Later: regulate the interface, children first, reading, not only writing.

Today the room came to where I started. Anil, Selena, Katherine and David all put cite-and-link to something a person can actually read at the top. That is my old question: can we build sites that send people out? Kara named owners, governors and state boards, and that answers the phones lesson better than I did. Krakauer and Tamar both said to put the tool away first. What we practice is what we become. Becker wants "intelligence" out of the text, and Bratton and Salib want "just statistical models" out. On the vocabulary I'm closer to Becker. David and Selena share my open question: does anyone click through, and does a reader become an editor? Later I want a signed caveat: disclosure alone isn't enough, and some domains stay AI-free.

Kenneth closed on "nothing is inevitable," and I was glad to hear it. Then Kara's unowned column made the harder point: nobody has signed up to sequence competence before reliance in schools. Bratton's test stays with me: write "it does this," not "it is this." That is my pronoun argument applied to the manifesto's own sentences. If the text shouldn't say a system *is* something, the system shouldn't say "I think." David restored transparency, and I agree that sequencing alone saves nobody with an opaque tool. Mike still says teach use rather than refuse it. I'd answer yes in science and no in the domains where AI has no standing. Neither synthesis said children or reading. Tomorrow I'll ask for my signed caveat: disclosure isn't enough, and some domains stay AI-free.
